qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Due to the hardness difference between δ-ferrite and tempered martensite, stress concentration readily occurred at their interfaces, inducing crack initiation. Once formed, cracks were captured by δ-ferrite and propagated into and along the δ-ferrite band, forming second cracks like deep valleys (Fig. 6); crack propagation into soft δ-ferrite could be blunted (high resistance).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides strongly retarded dislocation gliding, greatly enhancing yield and tensile strength; the WHR of QA-620 was apparently higher than other QA specimens at true strain 0.01–0.1.

interface_notes.value: Cracks propagated and were arrested along the δ-ferrite bands; second cracks observed in tensile fracture of QA specimens.

phase_evolution.value: Water-quenched plate (IQ-1050) annealed at 620 °C for 1 h: retained austenite fraction increased and reverted austenite nucleated and grew at martensite lath gaps with C and Mn diffusing into austenite and Al into martensite/ferrite; recovery decreased GND density. At 620 °C, carbides precipitate (below the ~617 °C A1 cementite precipitation point).

slip_behavior.value: Ductile deformation started in the soft phase (ferrite, austenite); carbides in QA-620 strongly retarded dislocation gliding, raising yield and tensile strength, while decreased alloy-element content in the matrix reduced lattice distortion of tempered martensite, raising deformability. TRIP effect (and TWIP effect) occurred during deformation.

overall_structure.value: Micro-laminated microstructure consisting of δ-ferrite bands and tempered martensite lamellar, maintained after intercritical quenching-annealing. After annealing, a large number of fine austenite grains (reverted austenite plus retained austenite) are widely distributed in the tempered martensite region. At the annealing temperature of 620 °C, carbides (considered to be cementite) precipitate and are widely distributed in the tempered martensite.

source.reason: Overall microstructure of the QA-620 sample described across the abstract, results (Fig. 3/Fig. 4) and conclusions.

unmapped_findings: The 620 °C annealed specimen (QA-620) is the only QA condition in which carbides (Cm, considered to be cementite) precipitated and were widely distributed in the tempered martensite, because 620 °C is below the A1 cementite precipitation temperature (~617 °C).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides strongly retarded dislocation gliding to greatly enhance yield and tensile strength, while the decrease of alloy element content in the matrix reduced the lattice distortion of tempered martensite to rise the deformability of the steel (positive to ductility).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides and the lower annealing temperature reduced the SFE of the austenite in comparison with QA-680; its austenitic stability was therefore lower than that of the 680 °C annealed specimen.

In the tensile fracture of QA-620, significantly smaller micro-dimples than other specimens were observed; river pattern (propagation of cleavage cracks) was stopped by ductile fracture areas (dimples). Cleavage and quasi-cleavage features were associated with δ-ferrite.
QA-620 austenitic mechanical stability constant k = 1.24 (Fig. 9c), intermediate between QA-680 (0.56) and QA-740 (1.47)/QA-800 (1.50), indicating a moderate TRIP effect.

More austenite underwent TRIP effect in QA-620 than in QA-680, which neutralized the improvement of ductility of QA-680 due to its lower GND density; hence total elongation of QA-620 (~44.0 %) was almost the same as that of QA-680 (~45.6 %).

For all QA specimens including QA-620, the austenite grain-size distribution decreased monotonically with increasing size, with around 90 % of grains smaller than 4.8 μm (most austenite grains <2.0 μm).

All annealed specimens including QA-620 exhibited three-stage work hardening characteristics, in which stages II and III resulted from the competition between dislocation gliding and TRIP effect combined with TWIP effect, according to their SFEs (between 20 and 40 mJ/m²).
